title: Do Not Tear Up My Earth
subtitle: Documenting women’s voices in Louisiana’s grassroots environmental movement, 1970–1990
credit: Presented by the T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History, LSU Libraries. A project directed by Peggy Frankland, with interviews by Peggy Frankland, Jennifer A. Cramer, and Sharon Dyer. Photography by Gabriella Mills, courtesy of Peggy Frankland.
intro:
Oral history excerpts from a project documenting women’s involvement in Louisiana’s grassroots environmental movement, first presented by the T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History in 2001.

Peggy Frankland, an environmental activist since 1982, directed the project and worked with the Center to conduct the interviews, beginning in 1999. Her goal was to gather stories for a book that would document the historical and cultural information so often left out of mainstream history. Together, Frankland, Jennifer A. Cramer, and Sharon Dyer interviewed leaders in the state’s environmental movement, most of them women. The work was aided by a grant from the Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities.

pages.title: Awakening
pages.lead_caption: Debra Ramirez, Lake Charles. Photo by Gabriella Mills, courtesy of Peggy Frankland.

blocks.caption: Sister Helen Vinton, New Iberia. Put a buffer zone for pesticides in place.

blocks.title: The same family
blocks.transcript: I guess I’ve always thought of us all belonging to the same family, really.

blocks.caption: Lorna Bourg, New Iberia. Established buffer zones for pesticides.

blocks.title: We deserve better
blocks.transcript: You know, for a state that I love so much, and to be proud to be from, it’s probably one of the most polluted, dirtiest places in the United States. And the people of Louisiana really, we deserve better than that, and we need to get better than that.

blocks.caption: Theresa Robert, Burnside. Responsible for the IT decision.

blocks.title: David and the goliaths
blocks.transcript: Because I think we have been the David in just about all of these battles. Unfortunately, the goliaths are people that are using our resources, our tax dollars, jobs that we have provided them. And they have tried to destroy us with our own resources.

blocks.caption: David and Goliath: an editorial cartoon signed “Norwood,” with the giant labeled “Waste Management.”
Debra Ramirez, Lake Charles. Lived next to petrochemical plants and fought several petrochemical companies over groundwater contamination.

blocks.title: Running from the plant
blocks.transcript: We’ve been having problems with the plant early on, because I remember when it would explode, we didn’t have an alarm but the whistle to go off. But the police would come in, I say police but the sheriffs would come, and they would tell us to hurry up and get out, and we ran. Sometimes we were in our sleeping clothes, barefooted, and we were running Old Spanish Trail where gators were. They had gators in there, they had moccasins crossing the road, because don’t forget we talking about swamp land.

pages.title: Hysterical Housewives
pages.lead_caption: Mary Tutweiler, New Iberia. Photo by Gabriella Mills, courtesy of Peggy Frankland.

blocks.caption: Wilma Subra, New Iberia. Organized and represented communities, and furnished technical data to numerous groups.

blocks.title: Hysterical housewives, raving idiots
blocks.transcript: The first thing when you get involved in these issues is the industry and the agencies didn’t want to hear from the community. They treated them as hysterical housewives, raving idiots, not a clue about what was going on. “How dare these people come in here and tell us how we should be doing our job? And how dare they think that we’re going to accommodate them when we’re trying to do our job?”

blocks.caption: Mary Tutweiler, New Iberia. Prevented the creation of a commercial solid waste landfill.

blocks.title: A meddlesome housewife
blocks.transcript: I wasn’t quite hysterical. I think the first thing I was called is a meddlesome housewife, and I kind of liked it, because that’s what I was. I was a housewife, I had a baby on my hip, and I was certainly going to meddle if they were going to meddle with me, which is, you know, trying to convince me that garbage in my drinking water was good for me.

pages.title: Why Women?
pages.lead_caption: Clara Baudoin, Carencro. Photo by Gabriella Mills, courtesy of Peggy Frankland.

blocks.caption: Rose Jackson, Belle Chasse. Fights issues in the chemical corridor; battled a hazardous waste landfill.

blocks.title: A mother’s child
blocks.transcript: Because they know that a woman is more stronger than a man, and once you mess with a mother’s child, you got a fight on your hands.

blocks.caption: Clara Baudoin, Carencro. Member of the Louisiana House of Representatives. With Flo Gossen, she brought about the closure of a commercial solid waste landfill.

blocks.title: I wasn’t backing off
blocks.transcript: I think a woman is going to take an issue and it’s not going away, because when you get . . . I know when I got on my soapbox with the landfill I wasn’t backing off . . . and then when I took on the oilfield facility, I wasn’t backing off. And so certainly I think women are more dedicated to seeing a project complete, and I wanted that landfill cleaned up, or straightened up, or closed, and I wasn’t going to stop until something happened.

blocks.caption: The sign on the fence: Lafayette Municipal Landfill, final closure, May 31, 1988.
Shirley Goldsmith. Founded CLEAN and was one of the first activists to emerge in Louisiana. Stopped an ocean incinerator and closed the Willow Springs Landfill.

blocks.title: Don’t tear up My Earth
blocks.transcript: And I’m a very, very spiritual person. I feel that this world was given to us as stewards, for us to take care of, and we’re not the ones that should be destroying it. I have a very strong belief in God, and this was God’s message to me: that you don’t tear up My Earth, it was given to you.

blocks.caption: Women Pioneers of the Louisiana Environmental Movement, by Peggy Frankland with Susan Tucker (University Press of Mississippi, 2013).

blocks.body:
“Do Not Tear Up My Earth” is an updated presentation, first created by the T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History in 2001, of excerpts from a project documenting women’s involvement in Louisiana’s grassroots environmental movement.

The University Press of Mississippi has since published Women Pioneers of the Louisiana Environmental Movement, a book based on these oral histories, by Peggy Frankland with Susan Tucker. The book traces the roots of this social movement amid Louisiana’s growing oil boom and explores the dynamics between gender, race, religion, human rights, health care, politics, science, economics, and industry.

All of the oral histories used in the book are held by the T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History, a division of LSU Libraries Special Collections. LSU Libraries Special Collections is also the repository for the Louisiana Environmental Action Network (LEAN) Papers (Mss. 4876). For more information, please contact Jennifer A. Cramer at jabrah1@lsu.edu.

Credits

Interviews by Peggy Frankland, Jennifer A. Cramer, and Sharon Dyer, beginning in 1999, with a grant from the Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities. Photography by Gabriella Mills, ca. 2000, courtesy of Peggy Frankland.
